meteorShower.title: How meteor showers form
meteorShower.summary: A comet keeps shedding dust along its orbit, gradually building a dust trail. When the Earth crosses that trail, the dust burns up in the atmosphere as a meteor shower.
meteorShower.credit: Orbits and geometry computed with astronomy-engine; body sizes are exaggerated so the geometry stays legible

moon.title: Tour the Moon: craters, maria and landing sites
moon.summary: Roam the near and far side with NASA's LROC colour imagery and LOLA elevation data. Rotate, zoom, and use adjustable raking light to read the Moon's real terrain.
moon.hint: Drag to orbit · wheel/pinch to zoom · arrow keys refine a site view · click a feature to descend
moon.credit: Surface imagery and terrain: NASA / LRO / LROC and LOLA (CGI Moon Kit); LOLA elevation drives both mesh displacement and fine surface shading
moon.readout: Sub-solar longitude {sunLongitude}° · Sun {sunElevation}° above this point · viewpoint {altitude} km

oceanus-procellarum.title: Oceanus Procellarum
oceanus-procellarum.body: The largest of the lunar maria, covering about four million square kilometres. It is not one crater but an ancient lowland flooded by basalt lava, which is why it counts as an ocean rather than a sea.

mare-imbrium.title: Mare Imbrium
mare-imbrium.body: An impact about 3.8 billion years ago excavated a basin some 1,145 km across, and lava later filled it. The ridges still visible around the edge are ejecta thrown out by that impact.

mare-ser-enitatis.title: Mare Serenitatis
mare-ser-enitatis.body: The dark basalt of the Sea of Serenity is roughly a billion years younger than the surrounding highlands. Apollo 17 landed on its eastern edge, in the Taurus–Littrow valley.

mare-tranquillitatis.title: Mare Tranquillitatis
mare-tranquillitatis.body: A basalt plain about 873 km wide, darker than the highlands because its iron- and titanium-rich lava reflects less light. It is also where humans first walked on the Moon.

mare-crisium.title: Mare Crisium
mare-crisium.body: An isolated circular mare about 555 km across, ringed by mountains. Sitting near the eastern limb, it librates in and out of view from Earth.

mare-orientale.title: Mare Orientale
mare-orientale.body: One of the youngest large multi-ring impact basins on the Moon, on the south-western limb where it is hard to see whole from Earth. Its concentric rings are a textbook impact-basin structure.

south-pole-aitken.title: South Pole–Aitken basin
south-pole-aitken.body: One of the largest impact structures in the Solar System: about 2,500 km across and 13 km deep, mostly on the far side. Chang'e 4 landed inside it, in Von Kármán crater.

tycho.title: Tycho
tycho.body: Eighty-five kilometres across and relatively young at about 100 million years, Tycho has the Moon's most conspicuous ray system — binoculars will show it on any full moon.

copernicus.title: Copernicus
copernicus.body: A 93 km complex crater with a central peak and terraced walls, formed about 800 million years ago. Its rays are fainter than Tycho's, which makes it a useful marker for dating lunar terrain.

aristarchus.title: Aristarchus
aristarchus.body: One of the brightest features on the near side, roughly twice as reflective as the surrounding mare. It sits on the Aristarchus plateau, next to the winding volcanic rille called Schröter's Valley.

clavius.title: Clavius
clavius.body: At 231 km across, Clavius is among the largest craters on the near side. It is very old: later impacts have flattened and pockmarked its floor, and a chain of younger craters overlaps its southern rim.

tsiolkovskiy.title: Tsiolkovskiy
tsiolkovskiy.body: A far-side crater whose floor is flooded with dark basalt, making it one of the most recognisable landmarks on the lunar far side. The far-side crust is thicker, so such dark floors are rare.

shackleton.title: Shackleton
shackleton.body: Near the south pole, where crater floors never see sunlight and rank among the coldest places in the Solar System, possibly preserving water ice. It is a focus for lunar south-pole exploration.

apollo-11.title: Apollo 11 landing site
apollo-11.body: In July 1969 Eagle touched down at Tranquility Base, and Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the surface. The descent stage, instruments and footprints are still there.

apollo-12.title: Apollo 12 landing site
apollo-12.body: In November 1969 Intrepid landed within walking distance of Surveyor 3, which had been sitting on the Ocean of Storms since 1967. The crew brought parts of it home, so it is the only spacecraft ever visited on another world.

apollo-14.title: Apollo 14 landing site
apollo-14.body: In February 1971 Shepard and Mitchell came down in the Fra Mauro highlands, the terrain Apollo 13 had been aiming for. They climbed Cone crater on foot, hauling a hand cart of samples up the slope.

apollo-15.title: Apollo 15 landing site
apollo-15.body: In July 1971 Scott and Irwin landed at Hadley–Apennine, between the Apennine mountains and Hadley Rille, and drove the first Lunar Roving Vehicle. They returned the Genesis Rock, an anorthosite dating to the Moon's original crust.

apollo-16.title: Apollo 16 landing site
apollo-16.body: In April 1972 Young and Duke set down in the Descartes highlands, expecting to find volcanic terrain and finding impact breccia instead — a result that rewrote part of the lunar geologic map.

apollo-17.title: Apollo 17 landing site
apollo-17.body: The last crewed landing, in December 1972, came down in the Taurus–Littrow valley. Geologist Harrison Schmitt found the famous orange soil there, erupted about 3.6 billion years ago.

change-3.title: Chang'e 3 landing site
change-3.body: In December 2013 Chang'e 3 made a soft landing in southern Sinus Iridum, and Yutu became the first rover to drive on the Moon since 1976.

change-4.title: Chang'e 4 landing site
change-4.body: In January 2019 Chang'e 4 landed in Von Kármán crater, inside the South Pole–Aitken basin — the first soft landing on the far side. Yutu-2 is still roving.

change-5.title: Chang'e 5 landing site
change-5.body: In December 2020 Chang'e 5 sampled and returned 1,731 grams of lunar material from near Mons Rümker — the first sample return in 44 years.

luna-21.title: Luna 21 and Lunokhod 2
luna-21.body: Luna 21 landed inside Le Monnier crater on the eastern rim of Mare Serenitatis in January 1973 and deployed Lunokhod 2, which went on to drive about 39 kilometres — further than any other rover, and its wheel tracks are still visible from orbit.

apollo-11-tranquility-base.title: Tranquility Base, looking south-west
apollo-11-tranquility-base.caption: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. Photographed from about ten metres west of the Lunar Module Eagle's plus-Z footpad, looking toward the south-west at the crater rim Armstrong had spotted from the window during the descent.

apollo-11-armstrong-crater.title: Armstrong's crater from Tranquility Base
apollo-11-armstrong-crater.caption: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. A crater Armstrong called out during the descent, with the Lunar Module and flag at the left edge and the photographer's own shadow at the right.

apollo-12-surveyor-crater.title: Surveyor Crater from the rim
apollo-12-surveyor-crater.caption: Apollo 12, November 1969. Taken from north-east of Intrepid, sweeping west past the flag and then round into Surveyor Crater, where Surveyor 3 had landed two and a half years earlier.

apollo-14-fra-mauro.title: Toward the western horizon
apollo-14-fra-mauro.caption: Apollo 14, February 1971. A sweep across the Fra Mauro formation toward the western horizon, from the terrain Shepard and Mitchell crossed on foot.

apollo-15-hadley-rille.title: Hadley Rille and the Lunar Roving Vehicle
apollo-15-hadley-rille.caption: Apollo 15, August 1971. David Scott at the Lunar Roving Vehicle on the edge of Hadley Rille, photographed by James Irwin south of Station 2.

apollo-16-station-1.title: Station 1, Descartes highlands
apollo-16-station-1.caption: Apollo 16, April 1972. Charles Duke collecting samples at Station 1 while John Young photographs him, on the first moonwalk of the mission.

apollo-17-station-2.title: Station 2, Taurus–Littrow
apollo-17-station-2.caption: Apollo 17, December 1972. The second moonwalk: the parked Lunar Roving Vehicle and astronaut footprints across the valley floor, with the South Massif ridge beyond.

apollo-17-station-5.title: Station 5, on the edge of Camelot
apollo-17-station-5.caption: Apollo 17, December 1972. Boulders and the shoulder of the North Massif at Station 5, looking toward the massif. The strip covers most of the horizon but its two ends do not meet, so turning stops at the edge of the photograph.

change-4-farside-lander.title: The far side of the Moon, from Chang'e 4
change-4-farside-lander.caption: Chang'e 4, January 2019. The first panorama taken from the lunar far side: the lander's solar panels and the Yutu-2 rover's tracks inside Von Kármán crater, in the South Pole–Aitken basin.

eclipses.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
eclipses.summary: Solar and lunar eclipses both come from a near-alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon: the Moon's shadow sweeps Earth during a solar eclipse, while the Moon crosses Earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse. Switch sections to compare the umbra, penumbra and antumbra, and see why eclipses do not happen every month.
eclipses.hint: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · switch section and view in the control panel · space to play or pause · R to reset
eclipses.credit: Eclipse times, peak locations and body positions computed with astronomy-engine; the system view is schematic and not to scale

guide.title: Solar and lunar eclipse guide
guide.solarAlignment: At new Moon, the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth. A solar eclipse occurs where its shadow crosses the ground. Sizes and distances in this system view are schematic.
guide.solarPartial: From this observing site, the Moon gradually covers the Sun. During a partial eclipse, direct viewing requires certified solar protection; ordinary sunglasses are unsafe.
guide.solarTotal: Only when the Moon completely hides the photosphere does the corona appear. Its look is based on a 2024 photograph, while the overlap follows this event. Restore eye protection as soon as sunlight reappears.
guide.lunarAlignment: At full Moon, Earth lies between the Sun and Moon. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow on the side away from the Sun.
guide.lunarPartial: The Moon first crosses the faint penumbra, then enters the umbra. Here the umbra progressively covers its face, with the boundary following the calculated angular geometry.
guide.lunarTotal: Once wholly inside the umbra, the Moon appears copper-red from sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere. This colour is an illustration, not a brightness forecast.
guide.inclination: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1° to the ecliptic. Only a new or full Moon near an orbital node can line the three bodies up closely enough for an eclipse.

labels.sunAbout: The Sun is about 1.392 million km across, roughly 109 Earth diameters. Its mean distance from Earth is about 149.6 million km, a light-travel time of about 8 minutes 20 seconds. Because the Sun is a finite disc rather than a point source, shadows divide into an umbra, penumbra and antumbra.
labels.earthAbout: Earth’s equatorial radius is about 6378 km. During a lunar eclipse it casts a shadow away from the Sun; at the Moon's distance the umbra's radius is about 4600 km, roughly 2.65 lunar radii. The Moon can therefore fit wholly inside it, and the total phase of a long lunar eclipse can exceed an hour.
labels.moonAbout: The Moon’s radius is 1737.4 km, about 0.27 of Earth’s, and its mean distance from Earth is about 384,400 km. Its orbital plane is tilted 5.145 degrees to the ecliptic, so at most new and full moons it passes above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow and no eclipse occurs.
labels.umbraAbout: The umbra is the region from which the light source is completely hidden. Earth’s umbra has a radius of about 4600 km at the Moon; when the whole Moon enters it, a total lunar eclipse occurs. The Moon’s umbra is usually narrow where it reaches Earth, so the path of a total solar eclipse is narrow too.
labels.penumbraAbout: The penumbra is the region where the source is only partly hidden. A penumbral lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon enters only Earth's penumbra and misses the umbra, usually producing subtle shading. The Moon's penumbra covers a much wider area of Earth than its umbra, so partial solar eclipses are visible over a larger region.
labels.antumbraAbout: When the Moon's apparent diameter is smaller than the Sun's, the umbra closes before reaching Earth and the region beyond its tip is the antumbra. From there the Moon sits wholly inside the solar disc, leaving a brilliant ring. The sky does not darken as it does in totality, and the full corona is not visible.
labels.ascendingNodeAbout: One of the two points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the ecliptic, here moving from south to north. A new or full moon must occur near a node for an eclipse to happen. The node line slowly regresses westward, completing a circuit in about 18.6 years.
labels.descendingNodeAbout: The other crossing, where the Moon moves from north of the ecliptic to south. The period when the Sun is near the node line is an eclipse season. Each lasts about 35 days and repeats just short of six months later, usually producing two and occasionally three solar or lunar eclipses.
labels.eclipticPlaneAbout: The plane of Earth’s orbit around the Sun; its projection on the sky is the ecliptic, the reference for ecliptic longitude and latitude. Eclipses require the Moon to be near this plane, which is why the ecliptic's name is tied to eclipses.
labels.lunarPlaneAbout: The plane of the Moon’s orbit around Earth, tilted 5.145 degrees from the ecliptic. That tilt explains why eclipses do not happen every month: only a new or full moon near a node can produce one. Set the tilt to zero and every new and full moon produces some kind of eclipse.
labels.peakAbout: For a solar eclipse, greatest eclipse is the instant when the Moon's shadow axis passes closest to Earth's centre. This marker is the surface point intersected by, or nearest to, that axis then. It is usually near the centre path but is not necessarily the point of longest totality or annularity. The observer starts here and can be moved off the central path.
labels.observerAbout: The place you have chosen to stand. The discs in the observer view are drawn from this point’s horizon coordinates and the real angular diameters, so nudging the position is enough to turn a total eclipse into a partial one.

panel.title: Eclipses
panel.teachingNote: Teaching assumption: the Moon's orbit is set flat against the ecliptic. Its real tilt is about 5.1 degrees, so an eclipse requires new or full moon to occur near a node.
panel.sunBelow: The Sun is below the horizon here, so this place sees nothing. The discs above still show the real alignment.
panel.solarTotalityNote: During totality the Moon completely hides the Sun's bright photosphere, revealing the normally faint corona. Its appearance is based on a real photograph; the Moon's position, size and phase still follow the selected event's geometry.
panel.lunarTotalityNote: A totally eclipsed Moon appears copper-red because sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere still reaches it; shorter wavelengths are preferentially scattered along the way. The colour and brightness here are approximate.
panel.solarSafetyNote: Eye safety: except during the brief total phase when the Sun's photosphere is completely covered, looking directly at the Sun requires certified solar-viewing protection. Ordinary sunglasses are unsafe.
panel.solarImageCredit: Corona appearance: NASA/Keegan Barber, 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse; not a photograph of the selected event.
panel.lunarImageCredit: Lunar surface: NASA SVS / LROC WAC near-side map; Earth's shadow and red tint are dynamic illustrations.
panel.lunarSkyNote: The lunar eclipse as seen from Earth's centre: the Moon crosses Earth's penumbral and umbral discs, with the Moon and both shadow discs drawn at their angular sizes for that instant.
panel.solarSkyAria: The Sun and Moon discs as seen from the observer, drawn at their real angular sizes and separation
panel.lunarSkyAria: The Moon's disc and the Earth's shadow discs as seen from the Earth's centre, drawn at their real angular sizes
panel.scaleNote: The system view is schematic: body sizes are exaggerated separately and the Sun-Earth distance is heavily compressed (the real distance is about 389 times the mean Earth-Moon distance). Directions and instants come from the ephemeris.
panel.legendAria: Which phase each band on the timeline marks

stellarEvolution.title: Stellar evolution: where mass makes the branches
stellarEvolution.summary: Every star starts in a molecular cloud and a protostar, then burns hydrogen on the main sequence. After that, initial mass, mass loss and companions split the story into different endings. Follow the Sun’s branch, then see how a massive star reaches a supernova and branches again into a neutron star or a black hole.
stellarEvolution.hint: Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · ← → change stage · Space plays or pauses · R resets the view
stellarEvolution.credit: Models informed by NASA / ESO observations and visualizations; size, brightness and time compressed, color and structure enhanced; cards give representative physical values

appearance.title: Reading this visualization
appearance.molecular-cloud: Cold dust mainly obscures background starlight in visible light. Grey-brown filaments and knots are brightened here to reveal their structure; the cloud is not a glowing flame.
appearance.protostar: Dust surrounds a warm core, a rotating disk and bipolar outflows. The structure references Webb’s L1527 observations; those infrared images use mapped colors, and this is also not a naked-eye view.
appearance.main-sequence: The Sun appears nearly white from space. A warm-white photosphere, limb darkening and fine granulation represent surface convection. Granules and a few dark spots are enlarged, and rotation is accelerated.
appearance.red-giant: The cooler photosphere appears orange; large bright and dark cells indicate convection. Structure references ALMA observations of R Doradus, outside visible wavelengths. Color is a temperature-based illustration.
appearance.planetary-nebula: A blue-white central star illuminates nested gas shells. Their rims brighten where the line of sight crosses more gas. Cyan and warm red distinguish zones rather than universal true colors; the nebula is not a flat ring.
appearance.white-dwarf: A newly formed white dwarf is hot and blue-white. Over long cooling times it becomes dimmer and redder. A small, smooth photosphere sits inside a circle marking the Sun on the same compressed size scale.
appearance.supernova: Directional and density differences can exist from the explosion’s outset. Interaction with surrounding gas continues to shape the irregular debris. The flash and long-term remnant evolution are compressed here; blue and orange-red distinguish structures, not a universal shell shape.
appearance.neutron-star: A pulsar is shown as an example: tilted radiation beams sweep around as it spins. Blue field lines and beams are teaching overlays, not visible solid structures. Not every neutron star is observed as a pulsar.
appearance.black-hole: The central dark region is the shadow, larger than the projected event horizon. Curved rays intersecting one thin disk create the lensed images. As the view crosses the disk plane, the foreground disk narrows and the arcs and occlusion change continuously. The model assumes a non-rotating black hole, a distant observer and an ideal thin disk; colors, brightness and gas textures are illustrative.

sun.title: The Sun, in numbers
sun.lifetimeValue: about 10 billion years on the main sequence, 5.4 billion of them left

tracks.title: Two forks after the main sequence
tracks.solarEnding: First fork: the core never reaches iron; the envelope becomes a planetary nebula and a white dwarf remains.
tracks.massiveEnding: First fork: the iron core collapses and the star goes supernova. A second fork follows: a lighter collapsed core leaves a neutron star; a heavier one can form a black hole.
tracks.sunNeverSupernova: The Sun is 1 M☉, far below the roughly {limit} M☉ core-collapse scale. Its core will never burn as far as iron, so it cannot become a supernova, neutron star or black hole. The mass line is approximate, not a universal hard cutoff.

molecularCloud.name: Molecular cloud
molecularCloud.tagline: Where stars are born: cold, dense gas and dust
molecularCloud.body: The coldest and densest regions of interstellar space, a few tens of kelvin at most and a thousand times denser than their surroundings. Molecular hydrogen and dust grains gather here, and a single cloud can hold millions of solar masses. When some denser patch finds its own gravity stronger than the gas pressure holding it up, collapse begins — a star needs no trigger to be born, only time.
molecularCloud.feature1: Around 10–20 K, among the coldest places in the universe
molecularCloud.feature2: Mostly molecular hydrogen, with dust hiding the starlight behind it
molecularCloud.feature3: Up to 10⁵–10⁶ M☉, enough to raise thousands of stars at once
molecularCloud.sun: The Sun formed in a cloud like this about 4.6 billion years ago. Nothing of that cloud is left.
molecularCloud.readout: Molecular cloud · stars are born here · about 15 K

protostar.name: Protostar
protostar.tagline: Lit by gravitational contraction, not yet by fusion
protostar.body: The collapsing core spins faster and grows hotter as it shrinks, turning gravitational energy into light and heat — all of it from contraction, none of it from fusion. Its own leftover dust hides it, so it is nearly invisible in visible light and is found in the infrared instead. Infalling gas flattens into a disk, while the poles fire high-speed outflows along the magnetic field.
protostar.feature1: Powered by contraction, with a core still short of the 10⁷ K ignition line
protostar.feature2: Wrapped in a dust envelope, radiating mainly in the infrared
protostar.feature3: An accretion disk and bipolar outflows at the same time, the outflows carrying off angular momentum
protostar.sun: The Sun spent about 100,000 years here, then its core reached about 15 million K and hydrogen fusion began.
protostar.readout: Protostar · powered by contraction · about 100,000 years

mainSequence.name: Main sequence
mainSequence.tagline: Hydrogen fusion in the core: the longest, steadiest part of a star’s life
mainSequence.body: With the core at about 15 million K, hydrogen begins fusing into helium. The star now regulates itself: the heat from the core holds the outer layers up, and the weight of those layers holds the core in. That balance lasts tens of millions to tens of billions of years. About 90% of a star’s life is spent here, which is why most of the stars you can see are on the main sequence.
mainSequence.feature1: The core turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second
mainSequence.feature2: Hydrostatic equilibrium holds luminosity and radius steady for billions of years
mainSequence.feature3: More mass means brighter and shorter-lived: a 20 M☉ star lasts about 10 million years
mainSequence.sun: The Sun is here now. It has used about 4.6 billion of its 10 billion main-sequence years. It is a G2V star with a surface at 5,772 K.
mainSequence.readout: Main sequence · the Sun is here · 4.6 billion years in

redGiant.name: Red giant
redGiant.tagline: Core shrinking, envelope swelling, radius up to a hundredfold
redGiant.body: Once the core runs out of hydrogen, fusion moves out into a shell around it while the core itself contracts and heats up under its own weight. The outer layers swell to a hundred times their size and cool as they do — which is why the star is both enormous and red. When the Sun reaches this stage its radius will grow to about 100 solar radii, Mercury and Venus will be swallowed, and the Earth will be scorched.
redGiant.feature1: Radius out to about 100 R☉ while the surface drops to around 3,300 K
redGiant.feature2: The core contracts and heats while the envelope expands and cools, both at once
redGiant.feature3: The core goes on to fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, through a helium flash
redGiant.sun: In about 5.4 billion years the Sun becomes a red giant, swelling about a hundredfold. The Earth’s orbit will be inside its envelope.
redGiant.readout: Red giant · about 100 R☉ · lasting about 100 million years

planetaryNebula.name: Planetary nebula
planetaryNebula.tagline: The envelope drifts off as a glowing shell, baring a searing core
planetaryNebula.body: Once the red giant has burned through its helium there is nothing left to hold it up. Its pulsations grow violent and it throws off the whole envelope. The exposed core, now hotter than 30,000 K, floods the ejected gas with ultraviolet light and ionises it into an expanding, glowing shell. The name is a historical mistake: early observers with small telescopes saw a round disc and thought of a planet. It has nothing to do with planets.
planetaryNebula.feature1: The ejected gas glows because the central star’s ultraviolet light ionises it
planetaryNebula.feature2: The shell expands at tens of kilometres per second and disperses within tens of thousands of years
planetaryNebula.feature3: The central star exceeds 30,000 K and will soon cool into a white dwarf
planetaryNebula.sun: After its red giant phase the Sun will shed its envelope into a planetary nebula — a stage lasting only about 10,000 years, a blink on astronomical timescales.
planetaryNebula.readout: Planetary nebula · only about 10,000 years · nothing to do with planets

whiteDwarf.name: White dwarf
whiteDwarf.tagline: The Sun’s final home: Earth-sized, half a solar mass
whiteDwarf.body: When the nebula disperses, the core left behind is a white dwarf. It has packed about 0.55 solar masses into a body the size of the Earth, at roughly a tonne per cubic centimetre. It generates no energy at all; it shines on stored heat alone, and electron degeneracy pressure holds it up against its own gravity. It will simply cool, for longer than the universe has existed, into a black dwarf that no longer shines.
whiteDwarf.feature1: About 8,400 km across — close to Earth’s size — at about half the Sun’s mass
whiteDwarf.feature2: Held up by electron degeneracy pressure, with no fusion left at all
whiteDwarf.feature3: Capped by the Chandrasekhar limit of 1.4 M☉; beyond it, no white dwarf can hold
whiteDwarf.sun: The Sun will end as a white dwarf, and after that nothing dramatic will ever happen to it again. This is its real destination.
whiteDwarf.readout: White dwarf · the Sun’s destination · about 0.55 M☉

supernova.name: Supernova
supernova.tagline: How a massive star ends: the iron core collapses and the star blows apart
supernova.body: Stars born with roughly 8 solar masses or more usually enter the core-collapse branch (the boundary shifts with metallicity, mass loss and companions). Their cores can fuse all the way to iron; fusing iron costs energy instead of releasing it. The unsupported core collapses in under a second and throws off the envelope. A lighter collapsed core leaves a neutron star, while a heavier core or strong fallback can make a black hole. This is also where many heavy elements come from: the iron and calcium in your body were made in stellar explosions.
supernova.feature1: The iron core collapses in less than a second
supernova.feature2: Peak brightness of billions of Suns, outshining a whole galaxy for weeks
supernova.feature3: Scatters oxygen, silicon and iron into space as raw material for the next generation of stars
supernova.sun: The Sun is 1 M☉, far below the roughly 8 M☉ threshold, and its core will never burn as far as iron. It cannot become a supernova.
supernova.readout: Supernova · massive stars only · never the Sun

neutronStar.name: Neutron star
neutronStar.tagline: The collapsed core: a solar mass inside a dozen kilometres
neutronStar.body: After a supernova, if the collapsed core is still supported by neutron degeneracy (typically about 1.4–2 solar masses, with the upper limit set by the equation of state), protons and electrons are crushed into neutrons and a neutron star forms, barely twenty kilometres across. Its density reaches hundreds of millions of tonnes per cubic centimetre and its surface gravity is a hundred billion times Earth’s. Spinning furiously with an extreme magnetic field, it fires radio beams along its magnetic axis; when those beams sweep past Earth we call it a pulsar.
neutronStar.feature1: Only about 12 km in radius, at densities near 10⁸ tonnes per cubic centimetre
neutronStar.feature2: Rotation periods down to milliseconds, magnetic fields up to 10⁸ tesla
neutronStar.feature3: The magnetic axis is tilted from the spin axis, so the beams sweep past us periodically
neutronStar.sun: The Sun will never reach this: only a star that enters the core-collapse branch can leave a neutron star after a supernova.
neutronStar.readout: Neutron star · about 1.4 M☉ · only about 12 km across

blackHole.name: Black hole
blackHole.tagline: A heavier collapsed core: not even light escapes
blackHole.body: If the collapsed core is too heavy for neutron degeneracy to support (often from a star born above roughly 20 M☉ in simple models, but not at a fixed cutoff), collapse continues into a black hole. Its boundary is the event horizon, inside which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so nothing comes back out. We cannot see it directly; we find it through X-rays from its accretion disk, the motion of nearby stars, and the way it blocks background light.
blackHole.feature1: The event horizon is where the escape velocity reaches the speed of light — not a solid surface
blackHole.feature2: A 10 M☉ black hole has a horizon only about 29.5 km across
blackHole.feature3: The accretion disk is heated to millions of kelvin and radiates X-rays
blackHole.sun: The Sun will not become a black hole: it never reaches core collapse and has nowhere near the mass needed to push a collapsed core past neutron-star support.
blackHole.readout: Black hole · a 10 M☉ horizon is about 29.5 km

labels.molecularCloudAbout: A cold, dense cloud of interstellar gas and dust, a thousand times denser than its surroundings. Stars are born here.
labels.dustGrainsAbout: Tiny solid particles of silicates and carbon that block the starlight behind them, making a molecular cloud look dark and empty.
labels.gravitationalCollapseAbout: When a denser patch finds its own gravity stronger than its gas pressure, the core starts to shrink — and once it starts, nothing stops it.
labels.protostarAbout: A shrinking body that has not yet ignited fusion. Every bit of its light comes from released gravitational energy.
labels.protostarDiskAbout: Gas falling towards the protostar carries angular momentum, so it flattens into a disk and spirals in along it.
labels.bipolarOutflowAbout: High-speed jets along the magnetic field from both poles. They carry off angular momentum, which lets more gas keep falling in.
labels.dustEnvelopeAbout: The gas and dust still falling in, which hides the protostar in the infrared.
labels.sunAbout: A G2V main-sequence star, about 4.6 billion years old, with a surface at 5,772 K.
labels.coreFusionAbout: About 600 million tonnes of hydrogen fuse into helium here every second, and the energy holds the whole star up.
labels.photosphereAbout: The surface we see, at 5,772 K. This is the layer the visible light escapes from.
labels.referenceCircleAbout: A fixed circle with the radius the Sun has on the main sequence. The red giant swells past it; the white dwarf shrinks well inside it.
labels.redGiantAbout: An old star with a shrinking core and a swelling envelope: a hundred times the Sun’s radius, and cooler at the surface.
labels.expandingEnvelopeAbout: The outer gas, heated by the core and swelling outwards. In the end it is thrown off entirely.
labels.heliumCoreAbout: The core left behind when the hydrogen ran out. It contracts, heats, and fuses helium into carbon and oxygen.
labels.centralStarAbout: The exposed core after the envelope was shed, with a surface above 30,000 K.
labels.ionisedShellAbout: Gas lit up by the central star’s ultraviolet light, expanding at tens of kilometres per second.
labels.planetaryNebulaMisnomerAbout: A historical misnomer: early observers thought the round disc looked like a planet. It has nothing to do with planets.
labels.whiteDwarfAbout: A dense remnant held up by electron degeneracy pressure: about 0.55 M☉ in a body the size of the Earth.
labels.degeneracyPressureAbout: A quantum-mechanical resistance that does not depend on temperature, so a white dwarf stays up without generating any energy.
labels.shockFrontAbout: The shock wave from the rebounding core bursts through the surface and throws the envelope out at tens of thousands of kilometres per second.
labels.ironCoreCollapseAbout: Iron is where fusion stops. An iron core cannot generate energy, so it collapses into a neutron star or a black hole in under a second.
labels.luminositySpikeAbout: Peak brightness of billions of Suns, outshining an entire galaxy for weeks.
labels.neutronStarAbout: A body made of neutrons, only about 12 km in radius, at hundreds of millions of tonnes per cubic centimetre.
labels.pulsarBeamsAbout: Radio beams along the magnetic axis. As the star spins they sweep past the Earth like a lighthouse.
labels.magneticFieldAbout: Up to 10⁸ tesla — more than a trillion times the Earth’s field.
labels.eventHorizonAbout: The boundary beyond which even light cannot escape. The larger dark region drawn here is the black hole shadow, not the surface of the event horizon itself.
labels.blackHoleShadowAbout: Light capture and gravitational lensing create a dark region larger than the projected event horizon. The near-side disk crosses in front. Viewed from above the disk, its far-side images form a broad upper arch and a smaller lower arc; viewed from below, their vertical positions are reflected.
labels.blackHoleDiskAbout: Matter pulled into a disk by the black hole’s gravity, heated by friction to millions of kelvin and radiating X-rays.
labels.photonRingAbout: These thin rings beside the shadow come from light orbiting the black hole multiple times before reaching us. Successive images become thinner and fainter toward the shadow, distinct from the broad lensed disk images.

supernovaRemnant.title: Supernova remnant: the Crab Nebula
supernovaRemnant.summary: Explore the aftermath of an explosion through the pulsar, rings and jets, diffuse cloud, and outer filaments.
supernovaRemnant.hint: Drag to orbit · Scroll to zoom · Toggle structural layers
supernovaRemnant.credit: Inner geometry: NASA / F. J. Summers, R. L. Hurt. Clouds and filaments are teaching reconstructions; colors and relative scales enhanced.
supernovaRemnant.intro: The guest star seen in 1054 left this nebula. Its central pulsar still energizes the surrounding gas and high-energy particles.
supernovaRemnant.bandNote: Presets highlight structures prominent at each wavelength. These are not telescope images or a spectral simulation.

details.diffuse: Teaching reconstruction · Energetic particles emit synchrotron radiation in magnetic fields.

supernovaRemnant.loadError: The inner model could not load. Other layers remain available.
supernovaRemnant.empty: All layers are hidden. Enable a layer to continue exploring.
supernovaRemnant.science: The Crab is a pulsar wind nebula, continuously energized by a rapidly spinning neutron star. The pulsar and outer remnant coexist; they are not successive evolutionary stages. These rings and jets are not universal features of supernova remnants.
supernovaRemnant.reconstruction: The NASA model interprets the inner X-ray structure. The procedural outer filaments and diffuse cloud are informed by multiwavelength observations, not matched to measured positions. Color, scale and transparency distinguish structures. Auto orbit moves the viewpoint; it does not imply that the nebula rotates as a whole.
